usage: Use this exact line when you call your landlord or 집주인 about heating
Casual gripe to a roommate; 또 = again, very common
examples: 에어컨이 고장나서 너무 더워요.
The AC broke down so it's really hot.
고장나서 = because it broke; pairs with the result clause
세탁기가 고장난 것 같아요.
I think the washing machine is broken.
-ㄴ 것 같다 softens it to a guess, polite for reporting a problem
휴대폰이 갑자기 고장났어요.
My phone suddenly broke.
갑자기 = suddenly, natural with sudden malfunctions
nuance: 고장나다 is intransitive: the thing breaks on its own (machines, electronics, appliances). You say 'X이/가 고장나다', never 'X을/를 고장나다'. For a person breaking something on purpose or by accident, use 고장 내다 or 망가뜨리다 instead.
mistakes: Saying 'X을/를 고장났어요' — it takes 이/가, not 을/를, because the object is the subject that broke

usage: What you say to a repair person or building manager (관리실)
I sent it in for repair
수리 맡기다 = drop off for repair, e.g. a phone at the 서비스센터
examples: 보일러를 수리해야 돼요.
I need to get the boiler repaired.
Object takes 을/를; contrast with 고장나다 which takes 이/가
냉장고를 수리하는 데 얼마예요?
How much to repair the fridge?
-는 데 = the cost/effort of doing; useful for asking quotes
기사님이 내일 수리하러 오신대요.
They say the technician is coming to repair it tomorrow.
기사님 = the repair/service technician; -신대요 relays what the 관리실 told you
nuance: 수리하다 is the formal word you see on signs and invoices (수리비 = repair cost). In everyday speech 고치다 is more common for small fixes, while 수리하다 sounds slightly more official and is used for appliances, cars, and buildings handled by a professional.
mistakes: Using 수리하다 for fixing a relationship or a plan — that's 풀다 or 해결하다; 수리하다 is only for physical objects

usage: Say this when a delivery crew brings an appliance or you order internet
설치 기사 = install tech; very common with 인터넷/에어컨
examples: 에어컨을 설치하러 왔어요.
I came to install the air conditioner.
Said by the technician; -러 오다 = come in order to
이 앱을 설치하면 가스비를 낼 수 있어요.
If you install this app, you can pay the gas bill.
Also used for software, not just physical equipment
인터넷을 언제 설치할 수 있어요?
When can you install the internet?
Key question when setting up a new apartment
nuance: 설치하다 covers both physical installation (AC, shelves, washing machine) and installing software/apps. It implies setting something up so it's ready to use, unlike 놓다 (just placing). For uninstalling apps Koreans say 삭제하다 or 지우다, not 설치 취소.
mistakes: Confusing 설치하다 (install) with 설정하다 (configure settings) — you 설치 the app, then 설정 the options inside it

usage: Tidy up your room a bit
Classic line from a parent or roommate; 좀 softens the command
정리하다 + noun for arranging a specific space neatly
examples: 주말에 옷장을 정리할 거예요.
I'm going to organize my closet this weekend.
Common weekend chore; 옷장 = wardrobe/closet
냉장고를 정리하니까 공간이 많아졌어요.
After I organized the fridge, there's more space.
-니까 here = after doing and noticing the result
짐을 다 정리하고 나서 쉬었어요.
I rested after I finished sorting all my stuff.
-고 나서 = after completely finishing; 짐 = belongings/luggage
nuance: 정리하다 means putting things in order so a space looks neat, while 치우다 emphasizes clearing things away. You can also 정리하다 abstract things: 생각을 정리하다 (gather your thoughts), 일정을 정리하다 (sort out a schedule). For sweeping/vacuuming dirt, use 청소하다 instead.
mistakes: Using 정리하다 when you mean wiping off dirt — that's 청소하다 or 닦다; 정리하다 is about arranging, not cleaning grime

usage: Daily check before leaving home; note the ㅡ drops: 잠그+았 → 잠갔
Please turn off the gas valve
잠그다 also means shutting a valve/tap, not just doors
examples: 나갈 때 꼭 문을 잠그세요.
Be sure to lock the door when you go out.
꼭 = without fail; safety reminder for residents
수도꼭지를 안 잠가서 물이 계속 나왔어요.
I didn't turn off the tap so water kept running.
수도꼭지 = faucet; 잠그다 is the verb for taps
비밀번호로 폰을 잠갔어요.
I locked my phone with a password.
잠그다 also works for locking a phone/screen
nuance: 잠그다 has a ㅡ irregular: the 으 drops before 아/어 endings (잠가요, 잠갔어요), and it conjugates with 아 because the stem vowel ㅏ is bright. Beyond doors, it's the standard verb for shutting off water taps and gas valves. The opposite is 열다 (open) or 풀다 (unlock/release).
mistakes: Writing 잠궈요/잠궜어요 — the correct forms are 잠가요/잠갔어요 because the stem keeps ㅏ after the 으 drops

usage: First thing to say to the 관리실 about a leak
Water is leaking from the ceiling
에서 marks where it leaks from; common in older 빌라
examples: 화장실에서 물이 새서 아래층에 피해가 갔어요.
Water leaked from the bathroom and damaged the floor below.
Reporting a serious leak; 아래층 = the floor below
가스가 새는 것 같아요. 냄새가 나요.
I think gas is leaking. There's a smell.
Urgent line; 새다 also used for gas leaks
지붕에서 비가 새요.
Rain is leaking through the roof.
비가 새다 = rain leaking in; classic monsoon-season problem
nuance: 새다 is intransitive — the liquid or gas is the subject (물이 새다, 가스가 새다). The vowel ㅐ stays and the ending fuses: 새 + 었 → 샜어요. Don't confuse it with the homophone 새다 meaning 'to stay up all night' (밤을 새다); context and the object make it clear.
mistakes: Saying 물을 새요 — leaks take 이/가 (물이 새요), never 을/를, since nothing is doing the leaking on purpose

usage: Casual request to a roommate or partner
examples: 빨래를 베란다에 널었어요.
I hung the laundry on the balcony.
베란다 = where most Koreans dry clothes; 에 marks the spot
비가 와서 빨래를 못 널어요.
It's raining so I can't hang the laundry out.
못 + verb = unable to; rain blocks line-drying
건조대에 수건을 널어 주세요.
Please hang the towels on the drying rack.
건조대 = clothes drying rack, a household staple
nuance: 널다 is a ㄹ-irregular verb: the ㄹ drops before ㄴ, ㅂ, ㅅ endings (넙니다, 너세요, 너는). It specifically means spreading wet laundry out to dry on a line or rack. The opposite action, taking dry laundry down, is 걷다 (빨래를 걷다).
mistakes: Keeping the ㄹ in formal/honorific forms — it's 넙니다 and 너세요, not 널습니다 or 널으세요

english: to heat up / to warm up (food)
usage: Heat it in the microwave and eat
What a host or convenience-store clerk might say
Shall I heat up the soup for you?
examples: 남은 밥을 전자레인지에 데웠어요.
I heated up the leftover rice in the microwave.
남은 밥 = leftover rice; 에 marks the appliance
우유를 따뜻하게 데워 주세요.
Please warm the milk up nicely.
따뜻하게 = so it's warm; common adverb with 데우다
찌개를 다시 데워 먹었어요.
I reheated the stew and ate it.
다시 데우다 = reheat; -어 먹다 = do and then eat
nuance: 데우다 means warming up something that's already cooked or cooled, especially food and drinks. Don't confuse it with 덥다 (the weather/you feels hot) or 따뜻하다 (something is warm) — those are adjectives describing a state, while 데우다 is the action of heating. For cooking raw food from scratch you'd use 끓이다, 굽다, or 요리하다.
mistakes: Mixing up 데우다 (heat food) with 데다 (get burned) — 손을 데다 means you burned your hand

usage: Everyday chore request; 쓰레기통 = trash bin
I cleared out / vacated the room
Also means emptying a space when you move out
examples: 음식물 쓰레기통을 비워야 돼요.
I have to empty the food-waste bin.
음식물 쓰레기 = food waste, a separate bin in Korea
냉장고를 비우고 청소했어요.
I emptied the fridge and cleaned it.
-고 links the two chores in order
이삿날까지 집을 비워 주세요.
Please vacate the apartment by moving day.
집을 비우다 = move out / leave the place empty; 이삿날 = moving day
nuance: 비우다 is the causative/transitive partner of 비다 (to be empty). You 비우다 a container, room, or fridge — taking everything out of it. It also appears figuratively in 마음을 비우다 (let go / clear your mind). The opposite is 채우다 (to fill).
mistakes: Confusing 비우다 (empty it) with 버리다 (throw it away) — you 비워서 버리다: empty the bin, then throw the trash out

usage: I need to change the light bulb
전구 = light bulb; 갈다 = swap out a worn part
Common for 정수기 (water purifier) or AC filters
examples: 화장실 전구를 갈았어요.
I changed the bathroom light bulb.
Object takes 을/를; 전구를 갈다 = replace a bulb
정수기 필터를 6개월마다 갈아야 해요.
You should change the water purifier filter every 6 months.
마다 = every; routine home maintenance
배터리를 새것으로 갈았어요.
I replaced the battery with a new one.
새것으로 갈다 = swap for a new one; 으로 marks the replacement
nuance: 갈다 (ㄹ-irregular) here means replacing a consumable or worn part with a new one — bulbs, filters, batteries, blades. Don't confuse it with the identical-looking 갈다 meaning 'to grind/sharpen' (커피를 갈다, 칼을 갈다); the home-maintenance sense is 'swap out'. The ㄹ drops before ㄴ/ㅂ/ㅅ: 갑니다, 가세요.
mistakes: Saying 갈습니다 — the formal form is 갑니다 because the ㄹ drops before the ㅂ ending

usage: Safety check before leaving; 플러그 뽑다 = unplug
Pull the cord out of the outlet, please
examples: 외출할 때 가전제품 플러그를 뽑으세요.
Unplug appliances when you go out.
Energy-saving and fire-safety advice; 가전제품 = home appliances
충전기를 콘센트에서 뽑았어요.
I unplugged the charger from the outlet.
에서 marks where you pull it from
현금을 좀 뽑아야 돼요.
I need to take out some cash.
돈/현금을 뽑다 = withdraw cash from an ATM, very common usage
nuance: 뽑다 means pulling something out from where it's inserted — plugs from outlets, but also withdrawing cash from an ATM (돈을 뽑다), pulling weeds, or even selecting/picking someone. For unplugging, Koreans often just say 플러그를 뽑다 or 코드를 뽑다. The opposite, plugging in, is 꽂다.
mistakes: Using 빼다 vs 뽑다 — both can mean 'take out', but for plugs and cash 뽑다 sounds the most natural and idiomatic

usage: Check when an appliance won't turn on; opposite of 뽑다
Please plug it into the outlet
콘센트 = wall outlet; 에 marks where it goes in
examples: 충전기를 콘센트에 꽂았어요.
I plugged the charger into the outlet.
에 marks the destination; classic plug-in sentence
USB를 노트북에 꽂으면 돼요.
You can just plug the USB into the laptop.
-으면 되다 = it's enough to / just do; 꽂다 fits USB sticks too
꽃을 꽃병에 꽂았어요.
I put the flowers in the vase.
꽂다 also = stand something upright into; 꽃병 = vase
nuance: 꽂다 means inserting something so it stands or stays in place — plugs into outlets, USB sticks into ports, flowers into a vase, a book into a shelf. It's the natural opposite of 뽑다 (pull out). Note the spelling keeps ㅈ: 꽂아요, 꽂습니다, and don't confuse the verb 꽂다 with the noun 꽃 (flower), which sound similar but differ.
mistakes: Spelling it 꼽다 — the standard verb is 꽂다 (꽂아요/꽂았어요), though 꼽다 is heard colloquially
